This tiny speck of
light holds every human
being who has ever lived.
Every king, every war,
every love story,
all on a point
smaller than a single pixel.
It is called the
Pale Blue Dot,
and it may be
the most humbling photograph
ever taken.
In 1977, NASA launched
Voyager 1.
It swung past Jupiter
in 1979 and Saturn
in 1980, then kept
going, out toward the
edge of the solar
system, at about 38,000
miles per hour.
The astronomer Carl Sagan,
a member of the
Voyager imaging team,
had an idea.
Before the probe left
for good, why not
turn its camera around
and take one last
look back at home?
Pointing the camera so
close to the Sun was risky.
But on February 14,
1990, the team sent
the command.
From 3.7 billion miles
away, Voyager 1 took
60 frames, a family
portrait of the solar system.
In one of them,
caught inside a ray
of scattered sunlight,
was Earth.
Just 0.12 of a pixel.
A pale blue dot.
Thirty-four minutes later,
Voyager 1 switched off
its cameras forever,
to save power for
the long journey ahead.
Those were the last
pictures it would ever take.
The signal was so
faint and so far
away that it took
until May 1990 for
all of the image
data to reach Earth.
Sagan later wrote about
that image in his
1994 book, Pale Blue Dot.
Look again at that dot.
That is here.
That is home.
That is us.
Everyone we love,
everyone we have ever
heard of, lived out
their lives on what
he called a mote
of dust suspended in
a sunbeam.
Voyager 1 is still
out there, now in
interstellar space.
On November 18,
2026, it becomes the
first human-made object
to reach one light-day
from Earth.
A radio message from
us will take a
full day to get there.
From out there,
there are no borders
and no nations.
Just one small,
fragile world, and the
only home we have ever known.
Look at it closely,
and take care of it.
The full story of
our cosmic prison is
on Miya's Lab.
